one_line_reason: Four single-ingredient placebo-controlled RCTs directly test oral Siberian ginseng (Eleutherococcus senticosus) alone across fatigue, glycemic response, athletic performance, and elderly quality of life, with results that are predominantly null or mixed and one clearly negative finding.

selected.population: adults with chronic fatigue ≥ 6 months, no identifiable cause (n=96 randomized, 76 followed to 2 months)
selected.intervention: Siberian ginseng, oral, alone, vs. placebo
selected.why_selected: the primary chronic-fatigue trial directly testing the most common marketing claim for this ingredient; overall efficacy was not demonstrated in the full sample, though a subgroup with less severe fatigue showed a significant (unadjusted) benefit.

selected.intervention: Siberian ginseng, oral, single 3 g dose, 40 minutes before a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, compared with placebo and 7 other ginseng types
selected.why_selected: a clearly dosed, controlled trial showing Siberian ginseng specifically RAISED postprandial glucose (90-min, 120-min, and AUC) compared with placebo, an important negative/cautionary finding distinct from claims made for other ginseng species.

selected.population: highly trained male endurance cyclists (n=9, randomized, double-blind, crossover)
selected.intervention: Siberian ginseng, oral, alone, 7 days before each trial
selected.primary_outcome: substrate utilization (fat oxidation) and 10-km cycling time-trial performance
selected.why_selected: clean single-ingredient RCT with a clear dose directly testing a common sports-marketing claim (fat utilization/endurance performance) and finding no significant effect.

selected.population: elderly hypertensive, digitalized volunteers (n=20, randomized, double-blind)
selected.intervention: Siberian ginseng (E. senticosus) dry extract, oral, alone, 8 weeks
selected.why_selected: clean single-ingredient RCT with a clear dose showing a transient benefit (social functioning at 4 weeks) that did not persist to 8 weeks, in a clinically relevant older population.

blockers: Across these four single-ingredient RCTs spanning fatigue, glycemic response, athletic performance, and elderly quality of life, results are predominantly null or only transiently/subgroup positive, with one trial showing a clearly negative effect (raised postprandial glucose).

No consistent effective dose emerges: trials range from a single 3 g dose to 300 mg/day to 1200 mg/day, each testing a different outcome, so no dose-outcome pairing is corroborated by more than one trial.

Several other shortlisted records combine Siberian ginseng with other ingredients (vitamin E + Korean ginseng; a 9-herb menopause formula) or use an active-drug comparator (fluoxetine) rather than placebo, further limiting clean supporting evidence.

excluded_pmids.reason: Broad systematic review of 25 different plants/phytonutrients on HPA-axis hormones; Siberian ginseng's specific result is not detailed, and the review concludes effects are largely 'unclear' for most phytonutrients other than ashwagandha.

RCT of a vitamin E + Korean ginseng + Siberian ginseng combination for female sexual dysfunction; effect cannot be isolated to Siberian ginseng, and the primary FSFI outcome was not significantly different from placebo.
Study protocol/background paper for the HALT menopause trial; reports no results, and Siberian ginseng is only 1 of 9 ingredients in the tested multibotanical formula.
Reprint of the same HALT study design paper (16186076); duplicate with no results.

RCT comparing Siberian ginseng to fluoxetine (both added to lithium) in adolescents with bipolar disorder; compared against an active antidepressant rather than placebo, in a narrow psychiatric population, so it does not establish Siberian ginseng's own efficacy versus no treatment.
